title: Adab with parents
hookLine: a man asks who most deserves his good company, and hears one answer three times

lines: YOUR MOTHER. YOUR MOTHER. YOUR MOTHER.
cards: Your mother. Then who? Your mother.
Then who? Your mother. Then who?
Then your father. Abu Hurayrah reports the exchange in Sahih al-Bukhari. A man had asked the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, which of all people most deserves his good companionship.
He asked four times, and the answer didn't move until the fourth. Not a speech, not a list of virtues. One word, said again and again, until it couldn't be missed.

teach.b: Why say it three times? The hadith itself doesn't explain, but the Qur'an gives a picture. In surah Luqman, in Pickthall's translation: "His mother beareth him in weakness upon weakness."
The verse goes on to the weaning. The repetition sounds like a debt counted out loud. And the father isn't dropped.
He's named, and his place is real. Then how. In al-Isra, kindness to parents comes right after the command to worship none but Allah.

teach.h: NOT EVEN A SIGH OF IRRITATION.
teach.b: When parents grow old, the verse says, don't even say uff to them, the smallest sound of irritation. Pickthall renders the rest: "speak unto them a gracious word."
And the image of the wing: "lower unto them the wing of submission through mercy." A bird lowering its wing over its young; here the grown child does it for the parent.
The verse gives a du'a too: "My Lord! Have mercy on them both as they did care for me when I was little."
The adab has an honest edge. Surah Luqman says that if parents push a child to associate partners with Allah, the child shouldn't obey, but should still keep company with them kindly in this world.
Disagreement doesn't cancel kindness. So adab with parents isn't only obedience. It's company, a gracious word, a lowered wing, and a du'a, with the mother named three times.

how: Muslims treat kindness to parents as a duty that follows worship of Allah, cite the hadith naming the mother three times, and recite "My Lord! Have mercy on them both as they did care for me when I was little" for their parents, living or dead.

o: caring for parents only once they grow old
obeying parents in every single thing they ask
kind company and gentle speech toward your parents

games.q: the adab with parents — tap the pairs.

s: the hadith names the father first
your mother, your mother, your mother, then your father.
the Qur'an forbids even a sound of irritation to aging parents
al-Isra: don't say uff to them; speak unto them a gracious word.
kindness to parents ends if they don't share your faith
Luqman: don't obey them in associating partners with Allah, but keep company with them kindly in this world.

games.q: you ask the Prophet who most deserves your good companionship, and you keep asking. what do you hear?
o: your mother, your mother, your mother, then your father.
games.why: the answer stays the same three times before the father is named: the repetition is the lesson.

practice: Bring your mother to mind, or whoever mothered you, and if she's living and you can reach her, picture a call today and one gracious word you'd say.

If she has died, a hadith in Sahih Muslim counts a child who prays for a parent among the good that continues after death; if you pray, you can say the line from al-Isra: my Lord, have mercy on them both as they did care for me when I was little.
If the relationship is hard, simply hold her in mind with whatever mercy is possible today.

wordCard.voice: Adab with parents. Good companionship, gentle speech and a lowered wing of mercy, with the mother named three times before the father. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: mother, three times. And your father too. Tomorrow, the adab with neighbors.
